title: Parenting With a Hangover: How to Get Through the Day Safely
excerpt: Hungover with kids? The four real safety risks (driving, infant sleep, supervision, breastfeeding), a morning survival plan, and low-effort ways to get through the day with a toddler or baby.
metaDescription: Hungover parenting survival guide: the safety rules for driving, baby sleep and breastfeeding, plus low-energy ways to get through the day with kids.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** you can get through a day of parenting with a hangover, but the goal changes. It is no longer a good day; it is a safe, boring, low-effort day. Most of the misery (headache, nausea, tiredness, a short fuse) is unpleasant but not dangerous. The real risks are a few specific situations: driving kids while alcohol is still in your blood, sleeping in the same bed as a baby after drinking, leaving small children unsupervised near water or medicine while you nap, and feeding a breastfed baby before alcohol has cleared. Handle those four, lower your standards for everything else, and you will be fine.

**The quick rules:** If you might still be over the limit, do not drive the kids anywhere; get a ride or cancel. Do not bed-share with a baby or fall asleep on the sofa holding one if you drank last night. Keep young children where you can see them, and never leave them in or near water. Put your painkillers out of reach. Then drink water, eat something, put on a show, and plan the quietest day you can.

> **When to get help, not tough it out.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **See a doctor or get urgent care if** you have repeated vomiting and can't keep water down, confusion, a severe or unusual headache, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, or blood in vomit or stool. If you feel too unwell or too impaired to keep a child safe, that is the moment to call your partner, a relative, a friend, or a neighbor, not to push through. If an adult is very confused, can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, or has blue-tinged lips, call 911; that can be alcohol poisoning, and it is an emergency. If a child may have swallowed alcohol or any medicine, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they seem fine.

## First, Check Whether You're Hungover or Still Drunk

This matters more for parents than for anyone else. A late night that ended at 1 a.m. can mean you wake at 6:30 with alcohol still in your blood. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, and nothing you do in the morning speeds that up: not coffee, not a cold shower, not a big breakfast. If you had six or seven drinks and stopped late, you may not be fully sober when the kids wake up.

Signs you may still be impaired, not just hungover:

- You feel giddy, slow, or "floaty" rather than just tired and sore.
- Your balance is off when you stand or walk down stairs.
- You can smell alcohol strongly on your own breath.
- You stopped drinking only a few hours ago and had a lot.

If any of those fit, treat the first few hours of the day as if you're still drinking. That means no driving, no cooking with hot oil, no bathing an infant on your own, and handing off as much as you can. Our guide to [driving hungover](/never-hungover/driving-hungover) explains why a hangover alone slows your reactions, and our guide on [how long after drinking you can drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) walks through the timing in more detail, and [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains why "I slept, so I'm fine" doesn't hold up.

## The Four Real Safety Risks of Hungover Parenting

Most of hungover parenting is about comfort and patience. These four are about safety, and they're worth getting right every time.

### 1. Driving kids while alcohol is still in your system

The school run is the most common trap. You feel rough rather than drunk, so you assume you're fine. But morning-after impairment is real, and a hangover itself slows reaction time and attention even after your blood alcohol has dropped to zero. If you're unsure, the safe options are simple: ask another parent to take your kids, use a ride service, walk if the distance allows, or let them miss the activity. A skipped swim lesson costs nothing. A crash with children in the car is the worst outcome on this list.

### 2. Sleeping with a baby after drinking

The American Academy of Pediatrics' safe sleep guidance specifically warns against bed-sharing with an infant when a parent has been drinking, and against falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. Alcohol makes you sleep more deeply and makes you less aware of a small body next to you. When you're hungover and exhausted, the risk of dozing off while feeding or cuddling is high. Put the baby down on their own flat, firm sleep surface, on their back, every time. If you feel yourself nodding off while holding them, put them down first and then rest.

### 3. Napping while young children are unsupervised

Toddlers and preschoolers can get into trouble fast: climbing, opening cabinets, wandering outside, getting into the bathroom. If you're going to nap, it has to be when someone else is watching the kids or when they're also asleep in a safe space (a crib, a childproofed room). Never nap while a young child is in the bath, in a paddling pool, or anywhere near water. Drowning can happen in a few inches of water and is usually silent.

### 4. Medicine and alcohol left within reach

Hungover parents often leave ibuprofen on the counter, a half-finished drink on the coffee table from last night, or a bag with pills on the floor. Alcohol is far more dangerous to small children than to adults because of their size, and even a small amount can drop a child's blood sugar dangerously. Before the kids are up, or as soon as you can, do a quick sweep: empty and rinse glasses and bottles, put them out of reach, and put painkillers back in a high or locked cabinet.

## A Survival Plan for the Morning: Getting Through the First Hours

Once safety is covered, the job is to feel a little less terrible while keeping the kids fed and reasonably happy. Here is a sequence that works for most people.

**Drink water before you do anything else.** Alcohol makes you pee out more fluid than you take in, and dehydration feeds the headache and the dizziness. Keep a big glass or bottle with you all morning and sip steadily. If you were sick in the night, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix helps more than plain water. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what to drink.

**Eat something simple, even if you don't want to.** Toast, crackers, a banana, eggs, or plain cereal. Low blood sugar after drinking makes you shaky, irritable, and foggy, which is the opposite of what you need with a toddler. Making the kids' breakfast and eating some of it yourself is a fine plan. For ideas, see [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

**Take a painkiller carefully, if you need one.** Ibuprofen with food is a common choice for a hangover headache, but it can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is gentler on the stomach but harder on the liver after heavy drinking. Take one standard dose of one product, follow the label, and don't stack it with cold or flu medicines that also contain acetaminophen. Our guides on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explain the trade-offs. Ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Coffee is fine, in moderation.** A cup of coffee can take the edge off the fog and, for regular coffee drinkers, head off a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. Too much can make the jitters and anxiety worse, so one or two cups is plenty.

**Get some daylight and air.** Opening the curtains, stepping into the garden, or a slow walk with the stroller often helps more than you'd expect. It also gives the kids something to do that asks very little of you.

## How to Parent a Toddler With a Hangover

Toddlers are the hardest age to parent hungover. They are loud, mobile, and need constant watching, and they have no interest in your headache. A few tactics help.

**Make one safe zone and stay in it.** Pick the most childproofed room in the house, close the doors, and set up there with toys, books, snacks, and water. You can lie on the floor or the sofa while they play around you. You are present and they are contained.

**Lean on screens without guilt.** One day of extra screen time doesn't hurt a child. If a favorite show or movie lets you sit quietly with a glass of water, use it. Save it for the toughest stretch of the morning, so it works when you need it most.

**Choose low-energy games.** Some ideas that let you stay mostly still:

- "Doctor" or "vet," where you're the patient lying down and they take care of you.
- Stacking blocks or building a train track while you sit beside them.
- A bath-free "water play" at the kitchen table with cups and a shallow tray, only if you're fully alert and right there.
- Stickers, crayons, playdough, or a sensory bin.
- Reading picture books while lying on the floor.

**Keep meals boring.** Pasta, sandwiches, fruit, yogurt. Nothing that needs you to stand at a hot stove for long.

**Get outside if you can.** A playground with a fence, a backyard, or a slow walk lets them burn energy while you do little. Fresh air also tends to ease nausea.

## Hungover With a Baby: Feeding, Holding, and Sleep

Babies need a lot of care but don't run around, so the challenges are different. The main risks are falling asleep while holding them and handling them when your coordination is off.

**Sit down for feeds and holding.** If your balance is wobbly, do most of your holding sitting on the floor or a low sofa, and avoid carrying the baby up and down stairs more than you need to.

**Don't doze with the baby on you.** Falling asleep with an infant on a sofa or in an armchair is one of the most dangerous sleep situations. If you're fighting sleep, put the baby in their crib or bassinet before you close your eyes.

**Bottle feeds are a good time to hand off.** If there's another adult around, overnight and early-morning feeds are an easy job to give away so you can sleep.

**Use the baby's nap.** When the baby naps in a safe sleep space, nap too. That is often the single best thing you can do for a hangover.

## Breastfeeding After Drinking

This deserves its own section because the advice is clear and a lot of people get it wrong. According to the CDC, alcohol passes into breast milk at roughly the same level as in your blood, and it leaves your milk as it leaves your blood. Waiting is what lowers it. The CDC notes that waiting at least two hours after a single drink before nursing reduces the amount that reaches the baby, and that "pumping and dumping" does not remove alcohol from your milk any faster.

What that means the morning after:

- If you had a lot to drink and stopped late, alcohol may still be in your blood and milk in the early morning. Use stored milk or formula for that first feed if you have it, and wait until you're clearly sober.
- If you need to relieve fullness and discomfort, it's fine to pump, but pumping is for comfort, not for clearing the alcohol.
- Once you feel completely sober, the alcohol has cleared from your milk as well, and you can nurse as normal.
- A hangover itself doesn't make breast milk unsafe. Once the alcohol is gone, feeling rough doesn't change your milk.

If you have questions specific to your baby, such as a newborn, a premature baby, or a baby with health problems, ask your pediatrician or a lactation consultant.

## Keeping Your Temper When Your Head Is Pounding

A hangover shortens your fuse. Noise hurts, you're tired, and many people feel anxious or low the day after drinking. That combination makes it easy to snap at kids who are just being kids.

A few things help:

- **Expect it.** Knowing you'll be irritable makes it easier to catch yourself before you yell.
- **Lower the bar on rules for today.** Messy floors, pajamas all day, and cereal for lunch are fine.
- **Take a 60-second break.** Put the kids somewhere safe, step into the next room, drink some water, breathe, and come back.
- **Use plain words with older kids.** "I'm not feeling well today, so we're having a quiet day" is honest and age-appropriate. You don't need to explain more than that.
- **Repair if you snap.** A quick "I'm sorry I was grumpy, that wasn't fair" teaches kids more than pretending it didn't happen.

The low mood and anxiety many people feel after drinking (often called "hangxiety") usually fade within a day. If it's strong, our guide on [hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why it happens. If low mood or anxiety stays with you well beyond the hangover, it's worth talking to a doctor.

## Getting Help: Partners, Family, and Tag-Teaming

The best hangover tool for parents is another adult. If you have a partner, agree on a fair swap: one of you takes the early shift so the other can sleep a couple of extra hours, then you trade. If you both drank, take turns rather than both trying to function at half power all day.

If you're parenting alone, it's reasonable to ask a friend, a grandparent, or a neighbor to take the kids for a couple of hours, or to come over so you can lie down. Many parents have done exactly the same thing and won't think twice.

What to hand off first, if you can:

1. Driving, until you're sure you're sober.
2. Bath time for babies and young children.
3. Overnight and early feeds.
4. Anything involving a hot stove, knives, or the pool.

## What to Skip Today

Some well-meant ideas make a parenting hangover worse:

- **Hair of the dog.** Another drink delays the hangover rather than ending it, and you're responsible for children today. Our guide on [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work) explains why.
- **Big outings.** A theme park, a long drive to relatives, or a crowded birthday party is a lot to manage when you feel this way. Move it if you can.
- **Hard exercise to "sweat it out."** You can't sweat out alcohol, and pushing hard while dehydrated can make you dizzy. A gentle walk is better.
- **Ambitious cooking or chores.** The laundry can wait until tomorrow.

## Planning Ahead: Avoiding the Next Parenting Hangover

Nothing guarantees a hangover-free morning except drinking less. That said, a few habits make a big difference when you know the kids will be up at dawn.

**Decide your limit before you start.** It's easier to stick to "three drinks and done by 10 p.m." than to decide in the moment.

**Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks slows your pace and keeps you more hydrated.

**Eat a real meal first.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol enters your blood.

**Stop early.** The earlier your last drink, the more sober you'll be when the kids wake up.

**Line up help in advance.** If it's a big night, agree who's on morning duty before you go out, or plan a sleepover at the grandparents'.

**Prep the morning the night before.** Lay out breakfast, fill the sippy cups, pick tomorrow's movie, and put the painkillers and water by your bed (out of children's reach). Future you will be grateful.

For a fuller list of what helps, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In

Some parents use a DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplement on nights out. DHM is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research so far comes from lab and animal studies, and human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers or makes you sober faster, so it never changes the rules above about driving, infant sleep, or breastfeeding. Some people find it a reasonable addition to the basics: eating first, drinking water, and stopping early. If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) are two widely used options, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it. If you're breastfeeding, pregnant, or take regular medication, check with your doctor before using any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Hungover parenting is mostly about getting through a long, slow day. Make sure you're actually sober before you drive or handle a baby alone, keep babies out of your bed and off your chest while you're drowsy, keep young kids supervised and away from water and medicine, and wait for alcohol to clear before breastfeeding. After that, drink water, eat something plain, take one careful dose of a painkiller if you need it, accept extra screen time, and ask for help. Tomorrow will be much easier.

faq.question: How do you parent with a hangover?
faq.answer: Aim for a safe, low-effort day rather than a good one. Make sure you're actually sober before driving or handling a baby alone, keep young children supervised and away from water and medicine, then drink water, eat something plain, set up one childproofed room, use extra screen time, and ask a partner, friend, or relative to take a shift if you can.

faq.question: Is it safe to drive my kids the morning after drinking?
faq.answer: Only if you're sure the alcohol has cleared. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, and sleep, coffee, or a shower don't speed that up, so a late heavy night can leave you over the limit in the morning. A hangover also slows reaction time on its own. If you're unsure, get another adult to drive, use a ride service, walk, or skip the trip.

faq.question: Can I sleep with my baby if I drank last night?
faq.answer: No. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against bed-sharing with an infant when a parent has been drinking, and against falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. Alcohol deepens sleep and lowers your awareness of the baby. Put your baby on their back on their own flat, firm sleep surface, and put them down before you rest.

faq.question: Can I breastfeed with a hangover?
faq.answer: Once the alcohol has fully cleared from your blood, it has also cleared from your milk, and a hangover itself doesn't make your milk unsafe. If you drank heavily and stopped late, use stored milk or formula for early feeds until you're clearly sober. The CDC notes that waiting at least two hours after a single drink reduces what reaches the baby, and that pumping and dumping doesn't remove alcohol faster.

faq.question: How do I entertain a toddler when I'm hungover?
faq.answer: Pick one childproofed room, close the doors, and stay there with toys, books, and snacks. Low-energy games work well: playing 'doctor' with you as the patient, blocks, stickers, playdough, or reading lying down. Extra screen time for one day is fine. A fenced playground or a slow walk lets them burn energy while you do little.

faq.question: What painkiller can I take for a hangover while looking after kids?
faq.answer: Ibuprofen with food or acetaminophen (Tylenol) are the usual options, but each has trade-offs after drinking: ibuprofen can irritate the stomach, and acetaminophen is harder on the liver after heavy drinking. Take one standard dose of one product, follow the label, avoid cold and flu products that also contain acetaminophen, and keep the bottle out of children's reach. Ask a pharmacist if unsure.

faq.question: When should a hungover parent get help instead of pushing through?
faq.answer: If you feel too unwell or impaired to keep a child safe, call a partner, relative, friend, or neighbor. See a doctor for repeated vomiting, inability to keep water down, confusion, chest pain, fainting, or a severe headache. Call 911 if an adult can't be woken or has slow or irregular breathing. If a child may have swallowed alcohol or medicine, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
